summary: This document specifies an RSA-based blind signature protocol. Blind signatures, first proposed by Chaum for untraceable payments, let a signer sign a message without seeing its content. The resulting signature can be verified as an ordinary RSA-PSS signature. It is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group.

eli5.summary: You put a note in an envelope with carbon paper. A notary signs the outside, and the signature copies to your note. The notary never read it, but the note is now stamped.

how do rsa blind signatures work
subtitle: Cryptographic signatures that hide the message from the signer.

tldr.problem: A sender wants a digital signature on a message, but wants to keep the message secret from the signer. Standard signatures reveal what is being signed.
tldr.mechanism: The sender blinds the message using a random factor, the signer signs the blinded message without seeing the original, and the sender unblinds the signature to get a valid signature on the original message.
tldr.outcome: Blind signatures enable privacy-preserving authentication in applications like digital cash and Privacy Pass, where the signer cannot learn what they are signing or create a link to later activity.

facts.label: Protocol interactions
facts.value: One round (client sends blinded message, server sends blind signature)

today: RFC 9474 is an Informational RFC from the Crypto Forum Research Group. It specifies a modern standardization of blind signatures for use in privacy-preserving systems. The protocol has been adopted in implementations of Privacy Pass and is under consideration for wider use.

sections.title: Introduction and Origins (Blind Signatures, Chaum)
sections.content:
RSA blind signatures were first introduced by David Chaum in the 1980s as a cryptographic primitive for untraceable digital payments. A blind signature protocol allows a client and server to cooperate in computing a signature on a message such that the server learns nothing about the message and the client learns the final signature without learning the server's private key.

This document specifies a modern instantiation of blind signatures using RSA-PSS encoding, a standard padding scheme used in TLS and other protocols. The resulting signature is a valid RSA-PSS signature that can be verified using standard libraries.
sections.eli5: Blind signatures let someone stamp your secret note without seeing what it says. You hide the message before sending it to them, they stamp it, and afterward you can reveal the signed message.

sections.title: Core Concepts and Use Cases
sections.content:
A blind signature protocol is a two-party protocol between a client and server. The client has a private message it wants signed. The server holds an RSA private key. The protocol executes in one round of interaction:

  • Client prepares the message and blinds it using a random value
  • Client sends the blinded message to the server
  • Server applies its private key to the blinded message
  • Server sends the blind signature back to the client
  • Client unblinds the signature to produce a valid signature on the original message

The key security property is that the server never learns the original message, yet the resulting signature is valid as an ordinary RSA-PSS signature. The protocol also prevents the server from linking multiple signatures to individual clients.

Blind signatures are used in privacy-preserving authentication mechanisms such as Privacy Pass, which allows users to prove their legitimacy without revealing their identity on each request. They also enable privacy-enhanced password-protected secret sharing schemes.
sections.eli5: The steps are simple: you mix your message with a secret number (blinding), the signer stamps the mixture without learning what is inside, then you remove the secret number (unblind) and have a real signature.

sections.title: The Protocol Steps
sections.content:
The RFC specifies four main functions. Prepare takes the original message and optionally adds random padding. Blind encodes the prepared message using EMSA-PSS (the padding from RSA-PSS), multiplies by a random blinding factor, and outputs both the blinded message and an inverse value.

BlindSign applies the server's private key to the blinded message using the standard RSA private key operation (RSASP1). It returns the blinded signature and also verifies that the operation worked correctly.

Finalize unblinds the signature by multiplying with the inverse of the blinding factor, verifies that the result is a valid RSA-PSS signature on the original message, and returns the signature.

The RFC defines four named variants. The randomized variants add fresh random bytes to each message, protecting clients from malicious signers that try to learn low-entropy inputs. The deterministic variants do not add randomness, useful when messages already have high entropy. Each variant specifies a hash function (SHA-384), salt length (either 48 bytes or zero), and preparation method.
sections.eli5: Step 1: Mix in the secret number. Step 2: Signer stamps the mixture. Step 3: Remove the secret number. Step 4: Check the signature is real. Done.

sections.title: Security Properties and Deployment
sections.content:
The blind signature protocol is proven secure under the one-more-RSA assumption, a standard assumption in elliptic curve cryptography. The security proof shows that an attacker cannot forge more signatures than the number of signing queries made to the server.

Two main security concerns are addressed in the RFC. First, side-channel attacks: the BlindSign operation is a direct call to an RSA private key operation, so implementations must protect against timing leaks using techniques like RSA blinding. Second, message validation: since the server signs without seeing the message, applications must prevent cross-protocol attacks by using a distinct signing key for blind signatures and ensuring signed messages are well-formed.

A subtle concern arises when messages have low entropy: a malicious server can construct an invalid public key to learn information about the client's input. The randomized variants protect against this by injecting fresh entropy into each message. For deterministic signatures, applications must ensure inputs have high entropy or verify that the signer's key is honestly generated.

The protocol is not post-quantum secure, as it relies on the hardness of integer factorization, which Shor's algorithm solves efficiently on quantum computers. The signature output is 2048 bits or larger, depending on the RSA key size.
sections.eli5: The biggest worry is that a tricky signer could learn your secret if it is too predictable, or a fast computer could read the secret by watching how long the signing takes. The fix is to add randomness to every message.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC provides guidance for implementors on error handling and key usage. Implementations SHOULD handle specific errors gracefully. The blinding step can fail with a blinding error (when the random factor is not coprime with the modulus), which is rare but should trigger a retry rather than failing the protocol.

Keys used for blind signatures MUST NOT be reused for any other purpose, including different RSABSSA variants. If a server supports multiple RSABSSA encoding options, it must maintain a separate key pair for each option. When the public key is carried in an X.509 certificate, it must use the id-RSASSA-PSS OID, not the generic rsaEncryption OID.

The RFC includes comprehensive test vectors covering all four variants, allowing implementations to verify correctness. The document specifies the exact hash functions, salt lengths, and message preparation to use for each variant, ensuring interoperability.
sections.eli5: Implementors must use fresh random numbers carefully, never reuse keys for different purposes, and use the exact method the RFC specifies so different implementations can work together.
